task: Adversarial review of KADS 0.9.0 (release/0.9.0, commit 28bd5a0): can a skeptical reader of a conforming corpus recover the KIND of basis behind a material claim, what ran, what was observed, the pass criterion, scope, inference, and what remains unverified?
reviewer: automated review (one agent); not verification by a person
documents_read: docs/research-guide.md (whole; the task named 'Assess tests consistently')
docs/clause-guide.md (tables for 1 to 8; examples for 1.4, 2.2, 3.1, 3.1 c, 3.2, 3.3, 3.4, 3.5, 7.1.5, 7.2.6, 8.2)
docs/authoring-guide.md lines 70 to 80; docs/learning-and-terminology.md lines 20 to 49
decisions/standards/KADS-J-010-verification-state.md and decisions/standards/evidence/2026-10-03-1/gate.json (for the recorded intent behind the 3.4 scope)
summary_verdict: Under the core alone (setting A), a claim that a SYSTEM was tested is bound only by 3.1 (a) 'identifiable basis' plus SHOULDs (3.1 b, 3.1 d) and two conditional MUSTs (1.4 when an evaluative word is used, 4.3 when the date is material). Clause 3.4, which would force what/against what/when, was deliberately scoped to 'documentation content' (gate finding, 2026-10-03), so a design page saying 'the OIDC flow was tested and works with provider X' conforms while the reader cannot tell whether an endpoint was called or a full flow ran, what was observed, or what criterion produced 'works'. Under the research-report profile (setting B) the distinctions are mostly recoverable; the residual hinge is that 'test report' in 7.2.3 is undefined, so a source review that mentions a trial in passing can escape it. Separately, the knowledge model's definition of Observation merges a source's assertion with a direct observation, which is a defect given 3.1 (a) and 7.2.5.

counterexamples.corpus:
docs/adoption-note.md:
  Follows KADS 0.9.0 (tag v0.9.0). Corpus: docs/. Profiles: none. Exceptions: none. Review route: the platform lead, on each release.

docs/login-design.md:
  # Sign-in design
  What this is: the design of sign-in for the web app, release 4, for its developers.
  Sign-in uses OIDC. The OIDC flow works with provider X: it was tested by the platform team against release 4 in September 2026, and "works" here means a user can sign in. The test itself was not recorded.
counterexamples.distinction_lost: Kind 2 versus kind 3, and everything inside kind 3. The reader cannot tell whether 'tested' means the documented endpoint was called once and returned something (direct observation), or the complete flow (discovery, redirect, token exchange, refresh, logout) was executed and assessed against the stated criterion. 'A user can sign in' names the criterion but not what was executed to satisfy it, what was observed, in which environment (staging? a developer laptop? production?), nor which provider X configuration. The reader also cannot tell what remains unverified, because 'not recorded' blankets the whole test. The scope of the conclusion ('works with provider X') is therefore unbounded relative to its evidence.

conformance_check.satisfied_because: The page opens by saying what it is, what it answers, and what it applies to.
Purpose ('design of sign-in') and scope ('release 4') are discoverable.

'Works' is an evaluative term that affects action; the corpus gives its criterion ('a user can sign in') within scope. 1.4 asks for the MEANING of the term, not for the execution record that applied it. The sentence also carries one meaning only.
No source document exists of which this sentence is a summary or derived view; 2.2 (a) and (d) bind restatements of a source, and there is none in the corpus.

The material claim ('works with provider X') has a basis of one of the listed kinds: 'an observation'. The basis is identifiable in the sense KADS uses elsewhere (6.3 b: 'identifiable even if access is restricted'): the reader can tell WHICH event is meant (a test by the platform team, release 4, September 2026) even though no artifact can be reached. The specification does not define 'identifiable', and the clause-guide gloss ('shows where it comes from') is satisfied by naming the team and month. A strict reviewer could argue that an unrecorded test is not identifiable; the text does not settle it, so the corpus conforms under a defensible reading.
(b) binds 'a citation'. No citation is made, so there is nothing to point at a passage or artifact. Omitting the citation altogether escapes (b).
No source is cited.
The claim rests on a method the page does not contain; the page says that it is not recorded ('The test itself was not recorded'). Satisfied literally.

The sentence states an observation-based claim with its basis in the same breath; nothing is presented as an inference or assumption that is not one. 'Wherever combining them would mislead' is a condition the author judges; a reviewer would need to show that 'tested ... works' combines an observation with an assessment in a misleading way, but 'assessment' is not one of the six kinds 3.2 lists, so the clause has no hook for it.
The claim is not unsupported; it has the stated test as support. (b) binds only unsupported claims.

Binds 'known' limitations. An author who never thought about production, token refresh, or a second provider configuration has none to disclose; the clause cannot reach limitations the author did not identify.
Nothing invented: the test happened, the team and month are true. (b): the missing record is marked ('not recorded').

The statement is that the OIDC FLOW (a system behavior) was tested, not that 'documentation content' was. See assessment_of_34_scope: the gate finding that produced the wording narrowed 'content' to 'documentation content' precisely so that a line such as 'Tested with browser X 120' is not caught. On the ordinary reading and on the recorded intent, 3.4 does not bind. Had it bound, the corpus would still satisfy it, because it states what (the flow), against which version (release 4), and when (September 2026).

Binds 'an artifact used to substantiate a material claim'. No artifact is cited or exists. Not citing an artifact escapes 3.6 entirely; the clause binds on citation, not on the existence of the evidence.
No configuration is presented as deployed state.

Compatibility with an external provider changes over time, so the date is material; the corpus gives month and release. (b): the method differs from current ones only if the author knows of a change; none is stated.
A design page, not a procedure.
No quantitative result.
The adoption note declares version, corpus, profiles, exceptions, and review route; a review record is assumed present in a real corpus and is not at issue.

counterexamples.missing_guarantee: A statement that a system, capability, or procedure was tested or executed (not only that documentation content was) says, or links to, what was executed, against which version or environment, and when or by which recurring process, or states which of these is not recorded. This is clause 3.4 (a) with its subject widened from 'documentation content' to the thing the content describes. Even that would not recover the criterion or the observed behavior; those are 7.2.3 (a) and are profile-only.

Because no evaluative word ('works', 'passed', 'verified') appears, clause 1.4 has nothing to bind. The reader cannot distinguish 'the test ran' (execution state) from 'the test passed' (assessment), which is exactly the separation the research guide asks for and 7.2.3 (a) enforces only under the profile. This corpus is better specified than A1 on date and environment and still hides the two things a skeptical reader would ask first.

conformance_check.satisfied_because: No evaluative term or score is used. 'Tested' describes an activity; it is not a score or an evaluative label within the clause's sense ('evaluative terms or scores'). A reviewer who wants to stretch 1.4 to 'tested' must argue that connotation is evaluation; the clause text does not say so.
Basis is an observation, identified by team, date, environment, and version.
No citation.

Departed from: the page neither says where the method is recorded nor that it is not. A SHOULD; the corpus still conforms. Adding 'test record not kept' would satisfy it without changing what the reader can recover.
As in A1. There is no 'assessment' kind in 3.2 to keep apart from 'observation', and the claim is supported.
Nothing invented.

A statement that the OIDC flow (system) was tested, not documentation content. If a reviewer applies it anyway, it is satisfied: what, against what, when are all present. Note that 3.4 does not require observed behavior or a criterion even where it binds.
No artifact cited.
Date, environment, and version are given.
No quantity.

counterexamples.verdict: conforms only by departing from a SHOULD
counterexamples.missing_guarantee: A statement that something was tested carries what was observed and the criterion against which it was assessed, or says that no assessment was made. In KADS this exists only as 7.2.3 (a) under the research-report profile; the core has no equivalent, and 1.4 is reachable only when an evaluative word is used.

docs/runbooks/rotate-oidc-secret.md:
  # Rotate the OIDC client secret
  For operators of the web app, release 4.
  1. Create a new secret in provider X's console.
  2. This step invalidates the old secret and cannot be undone. Update the app config and restart.
  3. Done when a test user can sign in.
  Verified: steps 1 to 3 executed as written against staging, release 4.0.2, on 2026-09-18, by the on-call engineer.
counterexamples.distinction_lost: Observed behavior and the criterion that turned the run into 'Verified'. This is a statement about documentation content, so 3.4 (a) binds and is satisfied; it is the shape the README and clause guide hold up as exemplary. But 'executed as written' is execution state, and 'Verified' is an assessment; the page does not say what was observed (did a test user sign in? did the restart complete?) nor whether the assessment criterion was step 3's completion condition or merely that the commands ran without error. A reader cannot tell a dry run that returned exit code 0 from a run in which step 3 was observed to hold. The J-010 operations challenger raised exactly this ('it conflates executed with verified') and the adopted clause did not take it up.

conformance_check.satisfied_because: 'Verified' is evaluative and consequential; its meaning is discoverable in scope by the clause itself (executed as written, against staging, on a date). Whether 'executed as written' is a criterion of success or only of execution is left open, but 1.4 asks for a discoverable meaning, and one is discoverable.
Basis: an observation (the execution), identified by date, environment, version, and role.

Observation and assessment are combined in one line, but 'assessment' is not a kind 3.2 lists, and the standard's own exemplar uses this form, so a reviewer cannot call it misleading under 3.2 without contradicting the clause guide.

Documentation content (the steps) was executed; the statement gives what (steps 1 to 3), against which environment and version, when, and by whom. Fully satisfied. 3.4 does not ask for observed behavior or criterion.
No edit is presented as revalidation.
Date and version given.
Prerequisites (implicit in scope), actions, and an observable completion condition (step 3) are stated.
The irreversible effect is stated in step 2.

counterexamples.missing_guarantee: A verification statement under 3.4 (a) distinguishes execution from assessment: it says what was observed and against which criterion the content was judged verified, or that only execution is claimed. No clause requires this in the core; 7.2.3 (a) requires it only for 'a test report' under the research-report profile.

docs/reports/oidc-provider-x.md:
  # Can release 4 sign in through provider X with OIDC?
  Question and scope: whether release 4 of the web app can use provider X as its OIDC identity provider. Scope: release 4.0.2, provider X documentation version 3.2, September 2026.
  Method: review of provider X's documentation (selection: the 'Authentication' chapter, read 2026-09-10) and a manual trial of sign-in by the platform team on 2026-09-18 against staging.
  Results: the documentation lists OIDC as a supported protocol. In the trial, sign-in through provider X completed.
  Reasoning: the documentation and the trial agree; the capability is likely suitable.
  Limitations: one provider configuration was tried; token refresh and logout were not exercised.
  Answer: supported, within the scope above.
  Sources: provider X documentation v3.2, 'Authentication' chapter (link).
counterexamples.distinction_lost: The criterion behind 'completed', and whether the trial was a single endpoint call or the complete flow. 7.2.1 is satisfied bullet by bullet, 7.2.5 separates the source assertion from the observation, 7.2.6 is honoured by the limitations line, and the inference is marked ('likely suitable'). What is not recoverable is the assessment: 'sign-in ... completed' reads as observed behavior but functions as a pass verdict, and no criterion is stated. 7.2.3 (a) would force the criterion if this is 'a test report'; the report presents itself as a source review with a trial attached, and 'test report' is not defined in the specification or Terms. The loss is narrower than in setting A and hinges on one undefined term.

conformance_check.satisfied_because: 'Supported' is bounded by the scope line; 'completed' is descriptive. No two meanings.
No derived view.
Two bases, each identified: an authoritative reference (cited to chapter and version, inspected) and an observation (dated, environment, team). The method is in the page, so (d) does not bind.
Observation ('completed'), inference ('likely suitable'), and answer are in separate labelled sections; limitations disclosed.
Nothing invented.
No statement that documentation content was verified; the trial is of the system.

No artifact (run output) is cited. Note that 7.2.1 'sources and provenance sufficient to assess the evidence' is satisfied by the method and sources lines on a lenient reading; a strict reviewer could ask where the trial's output is, but 7.2.1 asks for discoverability of provenance, not preservation of output, and 5.1 and 5.2 bind only where a corpus holds evidence.
Dates and versions given.
No quantity.

Each of the seven bullets is present: question and scope; method with inputs and environment; results separated from interpretation; reasoning from results to the conclusion ('agree; likely suitable'); sources; limitations; a current answer. The clause asks that these be discoverable, not that they be adequate.
A manual sign-in trial is describable enough for a suitably equipped reader to attempt (sign in through provider X against staging). (b): no barriers stated, and none are implied.

Binds 'a test report'. The term is undefined. The report is, by its own method line, a source review with a trial; 7.2's preamble lists 'investigation, experiment, benchmark, source review' as kinds of report, and 7.2.2 (a) says 'a source review need not invent an experiment'. If 7.2.3 is read as binding any report that reports a test, this corpus does NOT conform (no stated criterion; execution state and observed behavior are merged into 'completed'). If read as binding reports whose kind is a test report, it does not bind. The specification does not settle it.
The source assertion ('documentation lists') and the direct observation ('in the trial ... completed') are distinguishable; no inherited values.
No negative result is stated; the limitations line scopes what was not exercised, which is more than 7.2.6 asks.

counterexamples.missing_guarantee: A report that reports the execution of a test, under whatever heading, distinguishes execution state, observed behavior, and assessment against a stated criterion. 7.2.3 (a) says this but conditions it on the undefined phrase 'a test report'; the guarantee would be that 7.2.3 binds wherever a test outcome is reported, not only in a document of that kind.

docs/reports/oidc-provider-x.md: as in B1, with the Results line replaced by:

counterexamples.distinction_lost: The source assertion and the direct observation are now fused into one claim with two citations, and the trial is reduced to 'confirmed'. 7.2.5 says the two MUST remain distinguishable 'when that difference affects the claim'. The author of this line can argue that both bases agree, so the difference does not affect the claim; the condition is judged by the author, and a reviewer cannot show from the page that it was misjudged. The reader cannot tell what 'confirmed' consisted of.

conformance_check.satisfied_because: Both bases identified.
No inference is presented as observation in the Results line; the inference is in Reasoning.

'Observations or results separated from interpretation': the Results line reads as a result; 'supported' is the author's gloss on two bases, but it is placed in Results and nothing in 7.2.1 defines where a gloss stops being a result.
As in B1: undefined 'test report'. If applied, not satisfied.

The two bases are still nameable (documentation; trial), so a reader can distinguish them as sources; what is lost is the standing of each. The clause binds only 'when that difference affects the claim', and the author can state that the two agree.

counterexamples.missing_guarantee: 7.2.5 without its condition, or with the condition judged by the reader's need rather than the author's belief that the bases agree: a source assertion and a direct observation are stated separately whenever both support one material claim, because agreement between them is itself an inference the reader is entitled to check.

guidance_collapses.quote: **Observation:** what was recorded or reported by an identified source.
guidance_collapses.problem: Merges a direct observation (what was recorded) with a source assertion (what was reported by an identified source). The research guide, line 23, defines the same word more narrowly ('what the material directly records'); the authoring guide, line 72, keeps three bases apart ('Code can establish implementation behavior; a vendor reference can establish documented behavior; a test establishes an observation under recorded conditions'); 3.1 (a) lists 'an authoritative reference' and 'an observation' as different bases; 7.2.5 names 'source assertions' and 'direct observations' as things that MUST remain distinguishable. The knowledge model declares its list 'the one list of statement kinds KADS uses' (line 40), so an author who labels 'Observed: OIDC is supported (vendor docs)' is following the model, and the core has no kind under which a reviewer can object (counterexample A4). The defect is real but bounded: under the profile, 7.2.5 restores the distinction by name; under the core, nothing does. The model probably meant 'reported' to cover secondary records such as the archived transcript in the research guide; the sentence needs to say that the observation is then of the report, not of what the report asserts.

guidance_collapses.quote: This is the one list of statement kinds KADS uses; clause 3.2 names the ones that must stay distinguishable.
guidance_collapses.problem: The list has no kind for an assessment against a criterion (the third element of the research guide's 'Assess tests consistently' triad and of 7.2.3 a) and none for a source assertion or inherited value (7.2.5). Those profile clauses therefore distinguish things that the model says are not kinds of statement. The practical effect in the core is that 'tested and works' cannot be challenged under 3.2 (a), because the assessment it bundles with the observation is not on the list of things that must stay distinct (counterexamples A1, A2, A3).

guidance_collapses.quote: prefer a plain lead-in from one small set: Observed, Inferred, Assumed, Hypothesis, Recommended, Decided, Unverified.
guidance_collapses.problem: No lead-in for a source's assertion ('Reported' or 'Source states') or for an assessment ('Assessed' or 'Passed against'). An author who follows the advice has 'Observed' as the only lead-in for a vendor statement, which, combined with the knowledge-model definition, produces the A4 collapse in the standard's own recommended form.

guidance_collapses.quote: When you state that something was verified, reviewed, tested, or executed, give the check its shape: `Verified: <what was checked>, against <version or environment>, on <date>, by <who or what>` (clause 3.4).
guidance_collapses.problem: Two points. (1) 'something' is wider than the clause's 'documentation content'; the guide reads 3.4 as covering any tested thing, the clause does not, and the specification says the requirements take precedence over a guide. A reader of the guide believes system-test claims are governed; a reader of the clause knows they are not. (2) The shape has slots for what, against what, when, and who, and none for what was observed or against which criterion. It fixes execution plus verdict as the standard form, which is the A3 collapse.

guidance_collapses.quote:
Verified: steps 1 to 3 executed as written against staging, version 3.2,
on 2026-09-28. Not yet executed against production.
guidance_collapses.problem: The exemplar of the whole standard. It states execution state ('executed as written') and a verdict ('Verified') and omits observed behavior: it does not say that step 3's completion condition ('status reports serving') was observed to hold. The research guide asks to keep execution, observed behavior, and assessment apart; the README's model line keeps the first and third and drops the second, and the prose beneath it says this 'says exactly what "verified" means'. The same form is in docs/clause-guide.md line 333. Both are compliant with 3.4 (a); the collapse is in what the examples teach, not in what they violate.

guidance_collapses.quote: "Verified", "tested", or "executed" comes with what was checked, against what, and when, or says what is not recorded.
guidance_collapses.problem: The plain-words row drops 'documentation content' and, like the authoring guide, reads as if any 'tested' were governed. The row is informative and the clause takes precedence, but a maintainer checking a corpus against the table will believe A1 and A2 are caught by 3.4 when they are not.

guidance_collapses.quote: what was observed as against inherited, inferred, or assumed, by what method, with what limits, and what was actually verified
guidance_collapses.problem: The statement of the objective contrasts observation with inherited, inferred, and assumed, and leaves out 'asserted by a source'. Minor on its own, but it is the sentence the README points to for the objective 'in full', and the omission matches the knowledge-model definition: the two together make 'a source says X' indistinguishable from 'X was observed' at the level of what KADS says it is for. 7.2.5 lists the missing kind; the objective should too.

guidance_collapses.quote: Calling those cases failed tests solely because a request was rejected would confuse observed behavior with the assessment criterion.
guidance_collapses.problem: No collapse; recorded for completeness. The illustrative report keeps method, criterion, observed behavior, and assessment apart and says its table 'is a fixture for explaining assessment, not an execution log'. It is the best model in the repository for the distinction the core lacks.

guidance_collapses.quote: A method produces observations. An assessment interprets those observations against the criterion. / A human reply is still an assertion. ... Record the reply as an attributed statement and the result of trying it as a separate observation. / Distinguish an author's assertion from independent verification. / Have source assertions been presented as independently verified facts?
guidance_collapses.problem: No collapse here; recorded for completeness. These passages keep statements 1 to 4 apart correctly and are the right reference for a clarification elsewhere. The knowledge model is the odd one out.

uncommitted_draft_observed.note: While this review ran, docs/knowledge-model.md acquired an uncommitted working-tree change that I did not make (git diff at the end of the run: 7 insertions, 1 deletion). My review above is of the committed text at 28bd5a0. The draft is assessed here because it answers the same question.
uncommitted_draft_observed.what_changed: (1) The Observation bullet gains: 'A direct observation establishes what happened under the conditions it was made; a source's report establishes what the source says, not that it is so.' (2) A new subsection 'What a basis establishes' says what each 3.1 (a) basis establishes, calls a test result 'a composite: something was executed, a behavior was observed, and the behavior was assessed against a criterion', ties 'passed' to 1.4, and states: 'a statement that something was tested says what ran, against what, and when, or that this was not recorded (clause 3.4)' and 'Outside that profile the same separation comes from three core rules read together: the basis is identified (3.1), kinds of statement stay distinct where mixing them would mislead (3.2), and a verification claim says what it checked (3.4).'
uncommitted_draft_observed.assessment: The first change closes most of collapse 1: the word Observation still covers both, but the standing of each is now stated beside the definition, which is what A4 needed. The second change does not close the A1 to A3 gap and makes the guide/clause discrepancy worse. It asserts that 3.4 governs 'a statement that something was tested'; the clause binds 'a statement that documentation content was ... tested', and the gate record scoped it that way on purpose. It asserts that 3.2 keeps assessment apart from observation; 3.2 lists no assessment kind, and the knowledge model's own line 40 still says its list is 'the one list of statement kinds KADS uses'. It asserts that the core gives 'the same separation' as 7.2.3 and 7.2.5; counterexamples A1 to A3 conform to the core while losing that separation. An informative page that states the core's protection more firmly than the clauses do is the pattern clause 2.2 (d) warns against, applied to KADS's own guide; the specification says the requirements take precedence, so a reviewer who relies on this paragraph will pass a corpus the paragraph says is caught. If the normative change in 'recommendation' is adopted, the paragraph becomes true as to 3.4 and only the 3.2 sentence needs softening ('where mixing them would mislead' is the author's judgement, and assessment is not a listed kind). If it is not adopted, the paragraph should say that outside the profile the separation is recommended (3.1 b, 3.1 d) and conditional (1.4, 4.3), not required.

assessment_of_34_scope: Clause 3.4 (a) reads: 'A statement that documentation content was verified, reviewed, tested, or executed MUST say, or link to, what was checked, against which version or environment, and when or by which recurring process, or state which of these is not recorded.' The phrase 'documentation content' was not accidental. The gate review that admitted the clause (decisions/standards/evidence/2026-10-03-1/gate.json, finding on draft 3.3.5) listed as problem (4): "'content' is undefined: a product compatibility line 'Tested with browser X 120' is caught or not depending on the reader", and its fix was to 'scope "content" to documentation content'. The adopted reading is therefore that a claim that a SYSTEM, capability, or product was tested is NOT a 3.4 statement; the clause governs 'this procedure was executed', 'this page was reviewed', 'these steps were verified', and a review record under 8.5. The challengers in J-010 had argued the opposite direction (operations: 'it conflates executed with verified'; standards: 'the useful concept is exactly the part omitted: how the check was done, at a desk or on the real system'), and the gate kept a MUST only by narrowing. Consequences: (1) In a core-only corpus the sentence 'the OIDC flow was tested and works with provider X' is governed by 3.1 (a) alone as a MUST, and 'identifiable basis' is undefined; 3.1 (b) binds only a citation that exists and 3.1 (d) is a SHOULD, so a corpus that cites nothing and adds 'not recorded' satisfies every applicable clause while revealing nothing about what ran. (2) 1.4 forces the MEANING of 'works' or 'passed' when the word is used and is material, which usually yields the criterion, but it forces nothing about execution or observation, and bare 'tested' (A2) carries no evaluative term at all. (3) 4.3 (a) forces the date and version when 'material to a fact that changes over time', which compatibility with an external provider is; so date and version are usually recoverable in a conforming corpus. 4.3 (b) forces method and conditions only where they 'differ from current ones', which an author who knows of no change will not state. (4) 3.6 binds on a cited artifact; an author who keeps no artifact owes nothing under it. (5) Two informative texts (authoring guide line 80 'when you state that something was verified'; clause guide line 54) read 3.4 as wider than its text, and the specification says the requirements take precedence, so the informative layer overstates the protection. Net: the question 'was the system tested, what ran, when, against what' is answerable from a conforming core corpus only through SHOULDs and the author's judgement of materiality; the question 'was this documentation verified, what, when, against what' is answerable through a MUST. The asymmetry is not justified by the record: the gate's stated reason was the ambiguity of 'content', not a view that system-test claims need less support.
recommendation: normative change: 3.4 (a) binds a statement that documentation content, or the system, procedure, or capability that content describes, was verified, reviewed, tested, or executed; the required elements (what was checked, against which version or environment, when or by which recurring process, or which of these is not recorded) are unchanged. Detection stays as in J-010's admission test: text search for verified, reviewed, tested, executed, and works, then reading the sentence. It is breaking under 8.3 (c) (a core corpus with 'tested and works with provider X' becomes nonconformant until it adds a version, a date, or 'not recorded'), so at 0.x it increments the minor version and is marked breaking. It reverses the scoping choice recorded in gate.json for J-010; the proposal should cite that finding and argue that the ambiguity it resolved can be resolved in the other direction with one phrase. It does not recover observed behavior or criterion; those remain 7.2.3 (a), and moving 7.2.3 (a) into the core is not recommended (the J-010 challengers' cost objection applies with more force, and 1.4 already catches 'works' and 'passed' when material). Accompanying informative fixes, which are needed whichever way the normative question goes: (i) knowledge-model.md line 32, say that an observation of a report is an observation that the report says X, not an observation of X, and cross-reference 3.1 (a) and 7.2.5; (ii) authoring-guide.md line 78, add lead-ins for a source's assertion and for an assessment, or say that 'Observed' is not used for what a source states; (iii) authoring-guide.md line 80 and clause-guide.md line 54, align the wording with the clause's actual scope, whichever scope is adopted; (iv) README.md line 47 and clause-guide.md line 333, add what was observed to the exemplar ('status reported serving').
confidence_notes: The conformance checks apply the text as written; where the text leaves a judgement to the author ('wherever combining them would mislead', 'known limitations', 'when that difference affects the claim', 'material'), I took the author's defensible judgement, because a counterexample has to survive the author's good-faith reading, not a hostile one. Two hinges could flip a verdict: (a) if 'identifiable basis' in 3.1 (a) is read to require that the basis be locatable, A1 fails 3.1 (a) and the recommendation reduces to an informative clarification of 'identifiable'; I rate that reading less likely because 6.3 (b) uses 'identifiable' to mean nameable even when inaccessible and because 3.1 (b) exists to carry the locatability as a SHOULD. (b) If 'a test report' in 7.2.3 means any report that reports a test, B1 and B2 do not conform, and setting B has no gap beyond the author-judged condition in 7.2.5; I rate that reading about even with the other, which is itself the finding. The recorded intent behind 3.4's scope rests on one sentence in gate.json; I did not find a decision record that discusses system-test claims as such, so the claim that the asymmetry was unargued is an inference from absence in the files I read. I read docs/foundations.md line 11 (the objective) and grepped the examples directory for observation, assertion, criterion, and verification wording; I did not read docs/artifact-guide.md beyond its role table or the examples in full, so a collapse elsewhere in those files would be missed.
